newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil July trade deficit seen at $800 mln.
newsitem.headline: Brazil July trade deficit seen at $800 mln.

text.p: Brazil should post a higher-than-expected trade deficit of about $800 million in July, thanks mostly to strong oil imports, economists said.

Unofficial reports last week said the July deficit would reach about $800 million, significantly higher than the $570 million deficit forecast in a recent Reuter survey of Brazilian banks and research firms.
"The $800 million figure is not official, but these leaked figures are usually accurate," said Dany Rappaport, chief Brazil economist at Banco Santander.
The Ministry of Commerce and Industry is expected to release the July trade figures sometime this week.

Rappaport said unexpectedly high oil imports of about $600 million in July -- compared with a monthly average of $450 million during the rest of the year -- was the prime reason for the elevated deficit.
Economists said steady growth in raw material and capital goods imports due to an uptick in economic activity also pressured July trade numbers.
Brazil is also heading out of its coffee and soy bean export season, with coming months due to bring higher and higher trade deficits.
Still, July's number was not large enough to signal a trend change in import consumption, and economists said they would hold on to their year-end trade gap forecasts of about $11.0 billion.
"It would be imprudent to change year-end forecasts based on the July number," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief Brazil economist for J.P. Morgan.
"But if some economists were thinking about revising their year-end trade gap forecast below $10.0 billion, it might discourage them," he said.
J.P. Morgan forecasts a $13.3 billion trade gap for 1997.
Tomas Malaga, an economist at Brazilian retail bank Unibanco, said raw material and capital goods imports would continue growing this year, but not rapidly.

"There is still a lot of consumer default, so even though the economy is growing faster than the first half, we're not going to see a jump in raw material and capital goods imports," said Malaga. He forecasts a 1997 deficit of $11.4 billion.
Brazil posted a $5.5 billion trade deficit in 1996.
Economists pay a great deal of attention to the trade deficit because it is the chief contributor to Brazil's rising current account balance of payments deficit.
The current account gap, expected to hit about 4.5 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, is expected to rise above 5.0 percent of GDP in 1998.

Economists say Brazil should attract enough foreign direct investment and capital flows to finance the deficit at these levels. But they say the country cannot allow the gap to grow much further than 5.5 percent of GDP.
